name: Zinc-responsive Necrolytic Acral Erythema

ethnicAssociations: Predominantly reported in individuals of Middle Eastern and South Asian descent

criteria.description: Presence of well-demarcated, hyperpigmented, erythematous, scaly plaques localized to acral sites (hands and feet)
Low serum zinc levels or clinical improvement following zinc supplementation
Skin biopsy showing necrolysis of the upper epidermis with vacuolar degeneration and inflammatory infiltrate
Exclusion of other necrolytic erythemas such as necrolytic migratory erythema and pellagra

diagnosticCriteria.minimumForDiagnosis: All three major criteria (clinical presentation, zinc deficiency or response to zinc, and characteristic histopathology) must be met
diagnosticCriteria.notes: Diagnosis is often clinical supported by laboratory and histopathological findings; response to zinc supplementation is diagnostic and therapeutic

searchTerms: well-defined dark red scaly patches on hands and feet

laboratory: Normal or mildly elevated inflammatory markers
imaging: Not typically indicated; imaging usually normal
other: Histopathology showing necrolysis of upper epidermis with vacuolar degeneration and inflammatory infiltrate

distinguishingFeatures: Lesions typically involve perioral and intertriginous areas
Photosensitive dermatitis with Casal necklace distribution
Onset in infancy or early childhood
Periorificial and acral dermatitis with alopecia

redFlags: Rapid progression of acral lesions with ulceration
Failure to respond to zinc supplementation
Development of systemic symptoms such as fever or malaise
references: Sharquie KE, Al-Dhalimi MA, Al-Janabi AA. Zinc-responsive necrolytic acral erythema: a distinctive cutaneous manifestation of hepatitis C virus infection. Int J Dermatol. 2001;40(8):505-510.
